families.name: Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs)
families.definition: Probabilistic models of repulsion used to sample diverse subsets of items by balancing quality and diversity.

properties.text: DPPs offer efficient and exact algorithms for sampling, marginalization, and conditioning.
They model diversity as a statistical property rather than using heuristics.
DPPs can be integrated into large-scale, mature recommendation systems.
They are applied to top-N recommendation and YouTube content feeds to improve intra-list diversity.
DPPs on Knowledge Graphs can enhance diversity while ensuring a trade-off between accuracy and diversity.

limitations.text: The model's definition of diversity must match users' perception to avoid degrading user experience.
Integrating complex statistical models into large-scale systems remains challenging.

families.name: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)
families.definition: Deep learning architectures that model relationships between users and items in a graph structure to generate recommendations.

properties.text: GNNs characterize various relationships between users and items to model preferences.
Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become state-of-the-art for collaborative filtering.
Simplified GCNs (like LightGCN) remove feature transformation and nonlinear activation to improve performance.
GNNs can push diversification to the upstream candidate generation stage rather than post-processing.
Bayesian GNNs can recommend accurate and diverse items by handling implicit feedback uncertainty.

limitations.text: Standard GCN designs like feature transformation and nonlinear activation contribute little to collaborative filtering performance.
Processing the observed user-item interaction graph as ground truth can be problematic in implicit recommendation settings.

families.name: Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Bandits
families.definition: Online learning frameworks that optimize recommendation policies by interacting with users and receiving feedback to maximize long-term utility.

properties.text: Multi-objective RL balances conflicting objectives such as relevance, diversity, and novelty.
Bandit algorithms address the exploration-exploitation trade-off in preference elicitation and diversification.
Cascading Hybrid Bandits (CHB) model user behavior in ranked lists to maximize ranking utility for relevance and diversity.
Deep RL frameworks (like DRN) model dynamic news features and user preferences beyond simple click labels.
Linear Modular Dispersion Bandits (LMDB) learn personalized preferences on diversity properties of item sets.

limitations.text: One-by-one selection processes in some strategies are time-consuming for training and inference.
Greedy strategies in sequential selection rely on preceding choices being optimal or close to optimal.

families.name: Supervised Learning to Rank
families.definition: Methods that learn ranking functions from labeled data to explicitly optimize for diversity and relevance metrics.

properties.text: Supervised methods can produce superior results compared to unsupervised diversification methods.
Subtopic attention mechanisms explicitly model subtopics to diversify search results.
Structured learning frameworks can enhance both plain diversification and personalization performance.
Self-attention networks capture the interdependence of candidate document utilities during selection.
Supervised learning can treat each user as a training instance with heuristically chosen diverse ground-truth items.

limitations.text: Implicit approaches based on Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) may not explicitly model subtopics.
There is often a mismatch between the objective function used in training and the evaluation metric.

families.name: Post-Processing and Heuristic Diversification
families.definition: Techniques applied after candidate generation to modify the result list to increase diversity or reduce redundancy.

properties.text: Methods like MMR select documents one-by-one to balance relevance and novelty.
Simpson's Diversity Index from biology is adapted to ensure uniformity of item classes.
Sliding Spectrum Decomposition (SSD) captures user perception of diversity in long item sequences using time series analysis.
Heuristics are commonly used to diversify results in large-scale systems due to their simplicity.

limitations.text: Decoupling diversification from candidate generation makes the whole system suboptimal.
Heuristics are impoverished models of users' desire for diversity.
Greedy one-by-one selection is time-consuming and sensitive to local optima.

families.name: Fairness and Bias Mitigation
families.definition: Approaches that address biases in data and algorithms to ensure equitable treatment of users and item producers.

properties.text: Generalized Gini Indices (GGFs) are used to optimize for equality in item exposure.
Methods address selection, position, exposure, and popularity biases in observational data.
Fairness concepts are defined to balance relevance, diversity, and sustainability for consumers and producers.
Debiasing techniques aim to reduce the discrepancy between offline evaluation and online metrics.

limitations.text: User behavior data is observational, leading to inherent biases that blind fitting exacerbates.
Search systems create knowledge disparity and ill-decisions due to underlying data biases.

families.name: Explainable and Transparent Recommendation
families.definition: Systems that provide justifications for recommendations to enhance user trust, control, and understanding.

properties.text: Natural language user profiles offer transparency and scrutability of recommendation algorithms.
Knowledge graphs are used to post-process explanations for recency, popularity, and diversity.
Explainable hybrid recommendations display multiple explanation styles for each item.
Serendipity recommendations can be made directional and explainable to broaden user horizons.

limitations.text: Existing systems often neglect the properties of individual explanations and the diversity of explanation types.
There is a lack of work providing explanations specifically for serendipitous recommendations.
The accuracy-diversity dilemma remains a significant challenge, with no unified metrics for evaluating both simultaneously.
There is a lack of principled methods for evaluating the diversity of natural language generation systems.
Existing methods often assume static user preferences, neglecting the dynamic and multi-interest nature of users over time.
The trade-off between accuracy and diversity is not adequately addressed in domain-level and user-level adaptivity.
Blindly fitting observational data without considering inherent biases leads to serious issues like offline-online metric discrepancies.
It is unclear which evaluation metric is most suitable for specific search result diversification scenarios.
Integrating complex statistical models of diversity into large-scale, mature systems is challenging due to the need for alignment with user perception.
